title: Aditi, who arises with breath
theme: Aditi, made of the deities, who comes to be with breath and, having entered the cave, dwells there and was born with the elements — this is that.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «प्राणेन हिरण्यगर्भरूपेण»; Raṅgarāmānuja (quoting the Bhāṣyakāra): «प्राणेन सह वर्तते»

words.role: verb of the first relative clause

words.context: Śaṅkara: «शब्दादीनामदनात् अदितिः»; Raṅgarāmānuja (quoting the Bhāṣyakāra): «कर्मफलानि अत्तीति»

words.role: the one seen (object carried over from 2.1.6)
verb of the second relative clause

sandhi.rule: The s of aditiḥ becomes ru, P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः), heard as r before a voiced sound after i.
Final m → anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).

sandhi_exceptions.note: sambhavati aditiḥ: i before a is not turned into y. The words end the first pāda and begin the second, and both are counted (8 + 8). The base and Śaṅkara’s quotation of the verse print the vowels apart; the vishvAsa mūla and Madhva’s text write sambhavaty aditiḥ (corrections.json), which would leave the half-line with 15.

morphology.note: Feminine of devatāmaya, ‘consisting of the deities’, with the suffix -maya.

Accusative, with no verb in the verse to govern it: Śaṅkara supplies the seeing of 2.1.6. The mūla printed with Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary has the nominative tiṣṭhantī, and the Bhāṣya he quotes explains it so.
Imperfect middle of jan with vi: ‘was born variously, in many forms’.

translation.literal: ‘[He who sees] Aditi, who comes to be with breath, made of the deities, dwelling, having entered the cave, who was born with the elements — this, truly, is that.’
translation.readable: ‘Aditi, the eater, made of all the gods, who comes into being as breath, who has entered the cave of the heart and dwells there, and who was born together with the elements: this is that.’

anvaya: या देवतामयी अदितिः प्राणेन सम्भवति, या भूतेभिः [सह] व्यजायत, [ताम्] गुहाम् प्रविश्य तिष्ठन्तीम् [यः पश्यति सः एतत् एव पश्यति] । एतत् वै तत् ॥
syntax: Two relative clauses (yā … sambhavati; yā … vyajāyata) about Aditi, with the accusative guhāṃ praviśya tiṣṭhantīm depending on the ‘seeing’ of 2.1.6, which Śaṅkara supplies. The refrain closes the verse.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: Hiraṇyagarbha as breath, made of all the gods, called Aditi from ‘eating’ sound and the other objects, «शब्दादीनामदनात् अदितिः». Raṅgarāmānuja, quoting the Bhāṣyakāra on BS 1.2.11: the individual self, which ‘eats’ the fruits of action, «कर्मफलानि अत्तीति». Madhva, in a verse he cites: Viṣṇu, called Aditi from eating, «अदनादितिर्विष्णुर्यः प्राणसहितः स्थितः».

Raṅgarāmānuja: ‘that’ means ‘having that as its self’, «तदात्मकम् इत्यर्थः» — the individual self is ‘that’ because Brahman is its self, as the Gītā’s ‘know me as the field-knower’ is explained to mean ‘having me as its self’. Śaṅkara: this Aditi is the Brahman under discussion.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Two half-lines of 16 syllables (four pādas of eight, counting sambhavati aditiḥ unjoined), then the refrain etad vai tat, four syllables.

beginner: Aditi is an old name in the Vedas, the boundless mother of the gods. Here she is described as one who comes to be through breath, who is made of all the gods, who has entered the cave of the heart and lives there, and who was born together with the elements. The commentators read the name through a play on words: a-diti can be heard as linked to 'eating' (ad), so Aditi is 'the eater'. For Śaṅkara she is the first cosmic being, who 'eats' — that is, experiences — all the objects of the senses. For Raṅgarāmānuja, following the great teacher he calls the Bhāṣyakāra, she is the individual soul, who 'eats' the results of its actions. For Madhva she is Viṣṇu himself, born again and again in many forms. And again the refrain: this is that.
analogy: One tenant in many houses, called by a different name on every door.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Aditi, made of the deities, who arises with breath and, having entered the cave, dwells there, born with the elements — this is that.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Aditi is the one made of all the deities, «सर्वदेवतामयी सर्वदेवतात्मिका», who arises from the supreme Brahman as breath, in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, «प्राणेन हिरण्यगर्भरूपेण परस्माद्ब्रह्मणः सम्भवति»; she dwells in the cave like the first-born of 2.1.6.

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: He notes that the Bhāṣyakāra explained this verse under the sūtra on ‘the two in the cave’, «भगवता भाष्यकृता व्याख्यातः», and quotes him: Aditi is the individual self, who eats the fruits of action, lives with the breath, «प्राणेन सह वर्तते», and is born in many forms, as god and the rest, «देवादिरूपेण विविधा जायते». These are words of the Bhāṣya as quoted by Raṅgarāmānuja; Rāmānuja wrote no commentary on the Kaṭha.

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Madhva cites a verse (with «इति च», no source named) in which Aditi is Viṣṇu, highest of the gods, who brought himself forth in the cave in many forms, «मत्स्यकूर्मादिरूपेण», age after age; devatāmayī means ‘highest of the deities’, «देवतामयी देवतोत्तमा».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The base leaves sambhavati aditiḥ unjoined, keeping each pāda at eight; other witnesses join it. The accusative tiṣṭhantīm has no verb of its own here.

advaita.text: Aditi is Hiraṇyagarbha, the eater of all objects, «शब्दादीनामदनात् अदितिः», arising from Brahman; seeing her in the heart is seeing Brahman.

visistadvaita.text: Following the Bhāṣya he quotes, Aditi is the individual self, eater of the fruits of action, «कर्मफलानि अत्तीति»; ‘this is that’ means it has Brahman as its self, «तदात्मकम् इत्यर्थः».

dvaita.text: Aditi is Viṣṇu, called so from eating, «अदनादितिर्विष्णुर्यः प्राणसहितः स्थितः» (in a verse he cites), who takes many forms among beings.

schools.disagreement: One name, three referents: the cosmic first-born (Śaṅkara), the individual self (Raṅgarāmānuja, after the Bhāṣya on BS 1.2.11), and Viṣṇu himself (Madhva). All three hear ‘Aditi’ as ‘eater’.

parallels.note: The sūtra on ‘the two who have entered the cave’, under which, Raṅgarāmānuja says, the Bhāṣyakāra explains this verse.

contemporary.text: Three careful readers take one name three ways, each with reasons. The verse is a reminder that a text can hold more than one reading without any of them being careless. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: What in you ‘eats’ — takes in and lives on — the world?
reflect.deeper: Why might all three commentators hear ‘Aditi’ as ‘the eater’, and still disagree about who she is?
reflect.practice: At your next meal, notice how much of the day you spend ‘eating’ in the wider sense: taking in sights, words and news.

flags.note: sambhavati aditiḥ is written joined (sambhavaty) by the vishvAsa mūla and Madhva’s text (orthographic, corrections.json); the mūla printed with Raṅgarāmānuja reads tiṣṭhantī.
Aditi is Hiraṇyagarbha (Śaṅkara), the individual self (Raṅgarāmānuja, quoting the Bhāṣya) or Viṣṇu (Madhva).
